newsitem.title: JORDAN: Donors dig deeper for Palestinian refugee agency.
newsitem.headline: Donors dig deeper for Palestinian refugee agency.

text.p: Donor countries have averted an imminent cash crisis at the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, but the organisation which helps millions of Palestinian refugees said on Tuesday its finances remained precarious.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Peter Hansen said the donors, summoned to an emergency meeting in Jordan on Monday to tackle the agency's growing deficit, pledged an extra $14.5 million towards UNRWA's services.

He said the money had staved off the most immediate threat facing health, educational and relief programmes which the agency offers to its 3.3 million registered refugees in Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

But he urged the world community, especially oil-rich Arab states, to accept greater responsibility for the welfare of the refugees from two major Middle East Wars following the creation of Israel in 1948.

Hansen said before Monday's pledges of support, UNRWA was eating into the last of its reserves and looked like stumbling into 1997 with no working capital and enough money in hand to finance just two to three weeks' work.
Officials put the overall 1996 deficit at $45 million.

"Now with a little bit of money in the kitty, at least we won't go bankrupt tomorrow," he told a news conference. "If all the donors pay up we will make it through the year with a little working capital."
He said another $20 million of qualified pledges might materialise in the next two months, subject to parliamentary approval from the donor countries.

But he said the agency, facing spiralling costs because of its rapidly growing refugee population, needed more commitment from the international community to help reverse recent austerity measures which cut UNRWA to the bone.
UNRWA says the refugee population is growing by 3.8 percent a year.

"Children are now more than 50 in each classroom, recipients of the special hardship programme are not getting all the commodities they should, and each doctor in our clinics has 100 patients a day," Hansen said.
He called on the wealthy Gulf Arab states, their coffers swelled by a recent oil price surge, to follow the contributions of the poorer Arab nations hosting the refugees.

Hansen said contributions to UNRWA of Arab nations outside the host countries Jordan, Syria and Lebanon, had historically been low. But they plumbed new depths after Gulf states reduced aid to Palestinians because of their perceived support for Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"As of now Arab countries (outside host nations) bear only one percent of the burden of UNRWA," he said. "If rich Arab countries contributed 15 percent of UNRWA's budget, amounting to $60 million next year, we would not have a financial crisis."
The permanent status of the refugees is due to be settled under the final stage of a Palestinian self-rule accord between Israel and the PLO.

Israel disputes the number of people which UNRWA says were displaced in the 1948 and 1967 wars. Arab states say it is also resisting the right of return to Palestinians, and the election in May of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has further dampened hopes of progress.

"This refugee crisis is not the same as others," Hansen said. "We have here a population that has been dispossessed, their land, identity, dignity has been taken away, and they are the third or fourth generation of refugees."
